title.narrative: ROAF/Ethiopia/ Re-engineering Waste: Rehabilitating Dire Dawa's Landfill for a path to Safe and Sustainable Solid Waste Management Using the Fukuoka Method

description.narrative: Solid Waste Management (SWM) is a critical public service that directly affects public health, environmental sustainability, and economic productivity. Effective waste management safeguards communities, supports economic activities, and enhances political stability. Conversely, poor waste management leads to environmental degradation, health risks, and reduced urban efficiency. In Ethiopia, rapid urbanization and industrial growth have made SWM a pressing governance issue. Most municipalities struggle with limited waste collection coverage—formally collecting less than 50% of generated waste—while inadequate capacity prevents proper disposal and sustainable solutions. Dire Dawa, Ethiopia’s second-largest city with a population exceeding 366,000[1] (CSA projection, 2023), faces increasing waste generation due to rapid development and population growth. While infrastructure, institutional frameworks, and community participation efforts have expanded, the city administration struggles with resource constraints. Currently, only 48% of the city’s waste is collected, leaving 52% indiscriminately dumped in drainage lines, open spaces, streets, or burned. In 2005, a sanitary landfill was established on the urban periphery, but rapid city expansion has since encroached upon the site. Poor waste management practices—such as open dumping, lack of compaction, and inadequate leachate and gas collection—have turned the landfill into an environmental hazard, prone to fires, subsidence, and landslides. This project aims to rehabilitate Dire Dawa’s dumpsite into a safe and sustainable waste management facility using the Fukuoka Method. UN-Habitat will lead the initiative, leveraging partnerships with local and international universities, experts, and key stakeholders, including the Dire Dawa city administration, Dire Dawa University, UBS section, and SWAN Fukuoka (Japan). The project will apply the Waste Wise Cities Tool (WaCT) to assess waste flows, design an effective rehabilitation strategy, build local waste management capacity, transfer technology and expertise, and procure essential equipment. Through these coordinated efforts, the project will establish a long-term, sustainable SWM system, improving environmental health, reducing unmanaged waste risks, and serving as a model for other Ethiopian cities.
